Memorandum dated May 5, 1972, from Deputy Director, Bureau of Outdoor Recreation, U.S. Department of the Interior.
<u>Comment</u>: The memorandum asked for elaboration of the discussion on the impact of the program on land use.
The draft statement points out that in some cases most other uses of a particular tract of habitat will not be compatible with endangered species. Certainly, acceptance of those other uses whenever and wherever compatible with the production of endangered species will not only make the endangered species program more acceptable to the general public but will make more land available for habitat at less cost. Selection of those uses that could take place along with endangered species use will depend upon one or more of the following: (1) the requirements and tolerance of the endangered species involved; (2) whether the land in question harbors the only known population of the endangered species or is only one of two or more populations; (3) the health and status of this endangered species population; (4) whether endangered species use of the land is seasonal or yearround and whether seasonal use by endangered species coincides with the other use; (5) nature of the other use--does it exploit the habitat, involve human presence, change the cover, contaminate the environment, introduce competitors, etc.? Progressive improvement in the status of the species could actually allow more associated use of the area. The draft statement has been revised to more fully explain the impact on associated uses. BOR goes on to suggest that contrary to draft environmental statement, there may well be irreversible and irretrievable commitment of resources in achieving the goal of saving endangered species.
Response: We acknowledge the point and have revised the appropriate sections in the file amental statement.
